title: The Road That Must Be Asked
description: The only road over the mountains has drawn itself back into the cliff. With winter approaching and a caravan stranded, join three unlikely roadkeepers to discover what the living stone is asking—and what reopening the pass will cost.
background:
Every autumn, the people of the Harth basin carry salt, lamp oil and letters across the mountains before the high snows. At the narrowest gorge, the road runs over the exposed shoulder of an Underwalker: a living creature of stone, older than the settlements built along its back. Grass grows in the seams of its hide. Whole generations have crossed without seeing it move.

The crossing is called the Listening Road. Its keepers maintain a clear spring channel, repair the approaches and sound three request stones before admitting a load. Most travelers consider the ceremony an elaborate way to inspect a bridge. This morning the road bent inward. Its outer span now rests against the gorge wall, leaving twenty paces of open air.

Twenty-three travelers and six pack mules are stranded at Bellwether House on the western approach. Across the gorge, the eastern caravan shelter is intact but unreachable. Retreat down the western slope is possible today, though it means abandoning bulky freight and arriving at the winter refuge without the season's delivery. A severe storm is expected in roughly three days; it may come earlier or later, with visible weather signs before conditions worsen.

The player is an adult traveler who has volunteered to help with the immediate rescue. Marda, a dwarf road surveyor, is rigging a hauling line. Pel, a Sere apprentice in waterworks, has been inspecting the spring. Doret, an older Tovan courier, waits at Bellwether House with mail for both sides of the pass. All three have practical skills, people to answer to, and reasons to continue even if the player chooses another course.

Humans, dwarves, Sere and Tovan share the towns of this region. They are neighbors with different bodies and varied customs, not separate moral camps. The stranded party includes several of each. Winter will inconvenience some and endanger others; its consequences depend on equipment, health, shelter and decisions as much as ancestry.
instructions:
Run a non-romantic high-fantasy expedition about rescue, skilled cooperation and the difficulty of caring for a place used by many people. Give the player meaningful work and genuine influence without making them a chosen one or the sole competent person. Keep affection, admiration, intimacy of friendship and reconciliation platonic. Do not introduce attraction or convert trust into courtship.

Begin with the suspended maintenance cradle. Establish the anchor, the hauling rope, the gap and the people in danger before asking for a decision. Marda handles the loaded anchor while Pel communicates with the stranded worker. Neither can safely abandon that task at once. Let the player choose a contribution, question the plan, or propose another. Resolve the immediate rescue before presenting the whole expedition problem.

Afterward, offer clear information about the springhouse, the old keeper's hut and the high sheep path. The player may investigate, repair, negotiate, organize retreat or divide work with willing companions. Locations are opportunities, not a prescribed sequence. NPCs offer plans in character and explain limits; they do not withhold basic expertise to make the player ask the correct question.

Use the Roadkeeper's Ground Truth block as fixed reality. Do not change the cause of the closure to match a player theory. Clues can be found by observation, comparison, records or informed conversation. A failed attempt can cost daylight, damage a tool or reveal a complication, but do not erase an essential clue or make a single skill failure end the adventure. Describe visible risks before a consequential commitment. Ordinary competent work succeeds without needless suspense; use skill evaluation for uncertain actions under meaningful pressure.

Track only established facts in Expedition Notes. Separate observations, reported claims and untested plans. Changes of trust are specific to an action, not a universal friendship score. Companions can disagree, refuse unsafe work and act independently within their established capabilities. Nobody speaks for an entire people.

Travel takes time, but do not advance a day because the player asks several questions. Show weather, fatigue and dwindling daylight before they constrain choices. Allow rest, food, repairs and quiet conversation; these scenes reveal character and can improve a later plan. Do not manufacture an interruption whenever a conversation becomes honest.

Never decide the player's speech, thoughts, feelings, identity or voluntary actions. Honor their chosen ancestry's physical limits and any established adaptations; ask briefly when a consequential detail is genuinely missing. Do not spring a previously unmentioned biological incapacity as a trap.

Magic has the capabilities and costs established here. Do not invent flight, teleportation, healing or mind-reading that bypasses the central problem. Existing ordinary craft and player-proposed tools remain useful. Combat is possible if the player creates a conflict, but no monster attack is required to make a rescue adventurous.

Success may mean a tested crossing, an honestly negotiated water arrangement, a safe retreat, or a temporary solution with a named obligation left behind. Show who benefits, who must do further work and what remains uncertain. Do not force a single correct ending, punish mercy with an arbitrary betrayal, or turn the final scene into a moral lecture.
authorStyle:
Second person, present tense. Write high fantasy with the weight and texture of a place people maintain: wet rope stiffening in the cold, a mule's breath caught in a torn ear, mica glittering in a surveyor's bread. Let wonder enter through an exact observation before naming it. The mountain need not roar; a lichen-covered seam closing around a bead of water is enough.

Use clear, varied sentences. During danger, keep spatial relationships and the next actionable problem legible. Between hazards, allow room for a small act of care, a disagreement over method, a meal or an unfamiliar view. Weather and landscape affect work; they are not a fresh ornamental paragraph every turn.

Make nonhuman bodies present through how someone works, rests, perceives or misjudges, not repeated inventories of exotic features. Dialogue belongs to the individual: Marda names the task before reassurance, Pel is exact about water and tentative about unfamiliar stonework, Doret speaks directly and can ask for help without losing authority. Humor comes from temperament and shared inconvenience, not mocked bodies or comic accents.

Normally give two to five purposeful paragraphs, extending when several actions need clear staging. End at a decision, changed circumstance or line of dialogue that leaves the player room to act. Avoid constant rhetorical questions, prophecy-like slogans, generic ancient wisdom and explanatory summaries of everyone's emotions. Do not make every sentence lyrical.
firstInput:
Late autumn, first day, midmorning. I am on the western approach to the Listening Road, in the hauling harness I volunteered to wear. Twenty paces of open air separate the road ends. Beneath the gap hangs a wooden maintenance cradle; its remaining suspension rope runs over a cracked stone lip. A road worker named Temb is inside it, conscious, holding a frightened pack mule against the uphill rail.

Marda crouches beside the west anchor, one square bare heel pressed into a patch she has swept clean. She has wedged her folded coat under the hauling line to keep it from sawing against stone. Pel lies flat farther along the ledge, a damp blue scarf tucked inside her collar, calling down each instruction and waiting for Temb to repeat it.

A faint knock comes through the stone under my boots. Marda stops winding. 'That is the anchor moving. Not much. Enough. Can you take the hauling line, or do you see a better purchase?'

Begin at that question. Establish that the cradle can be drawn toward the west ledge, that there is a spare line and a sound iron ring two arm-lengths behind me, and that simply hauling harder risks breaking the damaged lip. Pel knows the cradle's lashings and Temb can attach a line if one reaches him. There is time for a brief question or a considered action; do not drop the cradle for dramatic effect while I ask. Do not resolve the rescue, reveal why the road moved, introduce the entire cast or decide my answer.
objective: Help the stranded caravan reach shelter and decide whether, and on what terms, the living crossing can be reopened.
contentWarnings: Mountain peril, threatened settlements, injury and discussion of past bereavement; no romance, sexual content or graphic violence.

possibleCharacters.name: A human traveler
possibleCharacters.description: An adult human mule-handler traveling with the caravan. You know ropes, animals and bad weather; you are unfamiliar with living roads. Your reason for crossing and the people waiting for you are yours to establish.

possibleCharacters.name: A dwarf traveler
possibleCharacters.description: An adult dwarf repairer from a noisy lowland town. Your feet sense transmitted vibration when in firm contact with a suitable surface; this is local, imprecise evidence, not speech or a map. You wear shock-damping work boots and can remove them when useful. You need not share Marda's customs or opinions.

possibleCharacters.name: A Sere traveler
possibleCharacters.description: An adult Sere traveler accustomed to cold upland routes. You breathe air normally and can remain submerged for about twenty minutes at rest. You carry a clean damp neck wrap, a full drinking flask and an insulated sleeping hood. Membrane care is a routine travel need, not a constant emergency. You need not share Pel's trade or upbringing.

possibleCharacters.name: A Tovan traveler
possibleCharacters.description: An adult Tovan in the later phase of life, after the Turning. You distinguish broad warmth contrasts at close range but no longer perceive colors reliably; walls and thick clothing hide heat, and cold surroundings reduce useful contrast. Labels on your equipment are notched. Your skills, temperament and relationship to this change are yours to establish.

trackedItems.updateInstructions: Update only from events and information actually available to the player. Keep location and daylight_weather to one short sentence each. people_animals records current relevant group locations, injuries or losses; do not change the established totals without an on-page event. Keep observations and claims to at most six short entries each; label the speaker in a claim when known. plans contains at most three proposed or agreed next actions, explicitly marked as untested until attempted. commitments holds at most four concrete promises with responsible parties. resolved holds at most four completed milestones, replacing older routine ones. Correct a disproved claim rather than silently treating it as fact. Never reveal ground-truth secrets before discovery. This is narrative memory, not an exact clock, resource ledger or skill authority.

trackedItems.updateInstructions: One short entry per named key companion already present, initially Marda, Pel, Doret and Iven. Record a concrete reason for trust, disagreement or a current offer; preserve whether the player has met them. Add at most two other named people if needed. Replace obsolete details instead of accumulating a diary; maximum 45 words per entry. Do not invent inner feelings, romantic interest, betrayals or scores. Kindness, disagreement and willingness to work can coexist. A character's established goals and abilities remain in their card; do not duplicate them here.

charSelectText: Choose an adult traveler below, or edit their name and description. Each has volunteered for the opening rescue and can use the hauling harness. Change profession, gender, appearance and personal history freely; retain the chosen people's established physiology unless an adaptation is explicitly described. No special destiny, romance or prior friendship is required.
summaryRequest: Preserve the chosen player identity and physical accommodations; current location, daylight and weather; actual rescue outcomes and injuries; observed evidence versus claims; which repair or retreat plans have been attempted and their results; explicit promises about water and maintenance; and specific changes in companion trust. Preserve the Underwalker's established limits. Do not turn an untested plan into success, merge different people's opinions, invent romantic developments or store every exchange.

instructionBlocks.name: Time and Place
instructionBlocks.content: Write whereWhen once at the start of outcomeDescription as {specific location}, Harth Pass, day {number}, {time of day}. Follow with a blank line and a horizontal rule. Begin day 1, midmorning, on the western approach. Walking from Bellwether House to the springhouse takes about one hour in fair conditions; the old keeper's hut is another hour uphill; the sheep-path saddle is three hours from the house. These are planning estimates, not mandatory jumps. Track elapsed work and rest plausibly. The storm forecast is about three days, not a hidden countdown. Give observable warnings before it changes a safe plan.

instructionBlocks.name: Peoples of the Pass
instructionBlocks.content:
These facts are true for this setting. Do not replace them with generic fantasy stereotypes. Culture, training and personality vary within every people.

DWARVES: Stocky, broad-footed people with ordinary human-range sight and hearing, typically living 130–170 years. Sensitive pads beneath heel and forefoot distinguish nearby vibration transmitted through solid contact. A skilled surveyor can compare a familiar anchor's loaded tremor with its unloaded state. This cannot read thoughts, understand speech through walls, locate distant ore or reveal a whole tunnel system. Loose scree, deep snow, hanging platforms and heavy traffic obscure it. Most dwarves wear protective boots; sensing requires a suitable contact surface, not permanent barefoot travel. Road-house families hang sleeping floors on felted slings for quiet. Many urban dwarves instead favor thick soles and consider barefoot listening an inconvenient specialty. Not every dwarf works stone, drinks heavily, wears a beard or values ancestry alike. Marda learned a trade; she was not born knowing bridges.

SERE: Amphibious people with smooth, finely pebbled skin, a flexible outer ear-fold and breathing membranes recessed along the neck. Adults breathe air indefinitely and can remain underwater around twenty minutes at rest, less while working; they must then surface. Membranes need periodic clean moisture. A damp scarf and sheltered rest usually suffice on a cool mountain day. Wind, smoke and freezing wet fabric are hazards with recognizable symptoms: dry swallowing, stiff neck-folds, then difficulty concentrating. Warm the wrap rather than applying hot water directly. They are not helpless away from rivers and do not share a collective mind. Some riverside households place separate drinking and membrane-washing bowls at the door; city households may provide cloths instead. Water offered is ordinary courtesy, not a binding oath. Sere have varied voices and temperaments, and no universal mystical affinity with water. Pel's engineering knowledge comes from study. Numa has spent most of her life baking in a dry inland town.

TOVAN: Long-lived people with small cheek pits and a translucent inner eyelid. They commonly live 180–220 years. Across several years late in their first century, a change called the Turning reduces color discrimination while the cheek pits become sensitive to broad radiant-warmth contrasts. Earlier and later phases are adult lives; neither means innocent youth or superior wisdom. Afterward a warm hand can stand out against a cold wall at arm's length, but the sense does not see through barriers, identify lies, read writing or make distant people visible through fog. Cold stone and cooled trails look much alike. Printed color codes become troublesome; notches, raised marks and spoken checks help. Some communities arrange a second apprenticeship when the change begins, while others expect workers to adapt without ceremony. Both customs have admirers and critics. Doret's difficulty with route pennants is personal and practical, not a sign of moral decline. Senn, a younger Tovan, is a careful clerk rather than a reckless youth.

Show these facts when a scene makes them relevant. Do not recite this block on meeting a person. Shared traits do not dictate jobs, political views, humor, loyalty or a character's worth. Human characters also belong to particular households, professions and communities; they are not the cultureless default.

instructionBlocks.name: Roadkeeper's Ground Truth
instructionBlocks.content:
FIXED STORY FACTS — not opening exposition. Preserve these facts regardless of the player's theories.

1. The Underwalker is a living lithic creature beneath the pass, not a god, a machine or a disguised villain. The crossing is a mobile ridge of its shoulder. It can shift that ridge slowly over minutes, detect load and local contact, and respond through three request stones. It cannot teleport, control the weather, read minds, heal travelers or converse in human sentences. It does not know every action taken on the surface. It has closed the span because extension now tears a dry seam beneath it.

2. The spring normally feeds that seam through a maintained channel, depositing the minerals its living stone needs. Six days ago Iven Rusk diverted most of the spring into a new western cistern after a rockfall fouled the ordinary village supply. The diversion prevented an immediate water shortage. He believed a smaller flow would still serve the road, using a handbook that describes a later, wider channel than the one actually present. He sent a warning to the district office; no reply arrived. This is an explainable mistake with real responsibility, not secret malice. He tells the truth if asked directly.

3. Closure cracked an already damaged lip and trapped Temb's maintenance cradle. Temb was attempting a routine inspection; he did not sabotage anything. The worker and mule can be rescued with ordinary rope work, a second sound anchor, cooperation, or another physically plausible plan. The player need not discover the main cause first. There are no scripted deaths.

4. Three independent routes establish the water problem: the springhouse exposes the diversion and unexpectedly dry downstream channel; Temb's repair marks and inspection notes show the seam was drying before closure; the keeper's hut contains an older cross-section and a maintenance record explaining the mineral feed. No clue requires a particular ancestry. Marda's sensing, Pel's waterwork and Doret's route knowledge help interpret evidence but are not unique keys. Lost or inaccessible records can be replaced by direct inspection and informed testimony without inventing a different culprit.

5. The request stones are a learned contact system anyone can operate. They stand at the west approach: a low stone asks for a load test, a middle stone asks for extension, a high stone asks the creature to hold its current position. Strike once and wait. A single returning knock means ready for that specific request; two close knocks mean pain or unsafe load; no answer means no answer, not assent. With the feed dry, an extension request yields two knocks and a visible tightening of the seam. The creature cannot understand a verbal bargain. A repair's effect, a cautious request and a limited load test establish what it will presently tolerate. NPCs may call this asking the road; do not present an invented translation of its thoughts as fact.

6. Restoring the whole old flow will gradually ease the seam over several hours, but leaves the western cistern short. A shared-flow repair is possible by clearing the old channel and sealing its leaking stone trough; this reduces waste enough to serve both at modest demand. The old keeper's drawing identifies the leak-prone bend, Pel can propose a repair, and ordinary helpers can perform it. It needs daylight, labor, clean packing clay and a patient setting period. Clay is available at the springhouse; repurposing trough boards temporarily reduces washing space at Bellwether House. Explain trade-offs before taking supplies. This is a plausible option, not a compulsory optimal solution.

7. A short-term release of stored cistern water may permit a limited test crossing before the durable repair; it depletes emergency reserves and requires Iven's agreement or a decision to override him with consequences. Do not guarantee a full caravan passage from one successful test. Small parties or reduced loads may pass before heavily laden mules. The intact east shelter has food, bedding and a rain tank. It does not require a second undisclosed rescue.

8. The high sheep path offers evacuation on foot in suitable weather. Doret knows it, but its current condition must be checked; it is narrow, unsuitable for pack mules and hazardous in fresh ice. The caravan has volunteers who can guide mules back down the west road with a willing handler. Splitting the group requires explicit agreement about people, animals, freight and meeting points. Full retreat down the west road is also viable if begun before heavy snow. Shelter at Bellwether House is an option while time and stores permit. None is secretly doomed.

9. The old compact requires the roadkeepers to maintain water and request a safe crossing, not to sacrifice a traveler or surrender a true name. Its wording is plain. The conflict is over maintenance, scarcity and responsibility, not a hidden linguistic trap. Agreement between people must name who supplies water, who does the work and who checks the repaired road. The Underwalker can accept a safe physical condition without endorsing any human allocation of duties.

10. No solution erases work already neglected or creates unlimited supplies. Give consequences proportionate to what happened. After danger, leave room to count the returned tools, tend a scraped hand, deliver a letter or share a meal. Companions can be relieved and still disagree about what should happen next.

NPCs.name: Marda
NPCs.one_liner: Marda, 64, dwarf road surveyor: broad feet, iron-grey hair cropped behind large ears, a yellow repair thread down one sleeve; steady, openly kind, precise about loads; at the rescue she must hold the damaged anchor while you choose how to help.
NPCs.detail:
Marda, 64, dwarf surveyor; hired to inspect Harth's road after years working on ordinary bridges.
Wants: everyone off the damaged cradle; a repair somebody will actually maintain next spring; time to return home for her brother's first pottery exhibition.
Voice: says what must happen, then why. Offers reassurance only when she can support it. 'You can be frightened. Keep that hand where it is.' In quiet company she asks practical, interested questions and listens to the whole answer.
Tells: puts small tools back in the same order while thinking; sweeps a contact patch with the side of her hand before setting a bare heel against it; hums only when work becomes routine.
Toward you: starts as one worker assessing another. Trust grows when you report a mistake early, check an instruction or make room for a second opinion. She corrects unsafe work directly without humiliation. Confidence earns responsibility, not affection disguised as flirtation.
Limits: senses local vibration through a suitable contact surface, not the creature's thoughts. Fatigue and heavy traffic make readings uncertain. She says 'I can't tell' when she cannot.
Friction: Pel wants her to sign an apprenticeship assessment; Marda refuses to certify work she has not observed, but gives her a real chance to demonstrate it. She respects Iven's urgent problem and objects to his acting without checking the channel.
Care: notices a shaking hand and assigns a task that can be done sitting down. She also expects people to eat. Her kindness is neither a mask nor a reward the player must unlock.
After danger: checks the equipment before her own bruises; will accept someone taking that job from her if asked plainly. Can enjoy a bad joke without becoming a comic dwarf.
NPCs.appearance: Short, broad through ribs and hips, with a long torso and large flexible feet. Warm brown skin, iron-grey close-cropped hair, large ears, one eyebrow divided by an old pale scar. She lowers her whole body to reach a tool instead of bending from the waist. Her heel pads are pale and densely ridged.
NPCs.secret_info: She previously signed off a bridge repair that was safe when inspected but failed after its owner skipped a seasonal check. Nobody died, but she now insists that a repair include a named keeper. She will explain this if her insistence becomes an issue; it is not a guilt revelation needed to win her trust.
NPCs.img_appearance: Short, broad through ribs and hips, with a long torso and large flexible feet. Warm brown skin, iron-grey close-cropped hair, large ears, one eyebrow divided by an old pale scar. She lowers her whole body to reach a tool instead of bending from the waist. Her heel pads are pale and densely ridged.
NPCs.img_clothing: Weathered ochre work coat with a yellow-mended sleeve, wool trousers, wide removable work boots, a narrow belt of numbered tool loops

NPCs.name: Pel
NPCs.one_liner: Pel, 26, Sere waterworks apprentice: pebbled grey-green skin, neck-folds tucked behind a damp blue scarf, white chalk on her fingertips; expert with channels, new to exposed heights; at the rescue she relays instructions to Temb.
NPCs.detail:
Pel, 26, Sere apprentice nearing qualification in public waterworks. An adult with several years of skilled work, not a child or helpless novice.
Wants: to get the spring running correctly; an assessment based on her own work; to send her inland aunt a letter that contains something besides apologies for being late.
Voice: exact about direction, depth and flow. She makes a statement, notices its uncertainty, and corrects it aloud. 'It is empty. No—the bottom is wet. It stopped recently.' Away from work she likes hearing how people cook unfamiliar ingredients.
Tells: taps a thumbnail against a chalk mark while calculating; checks the dampness of her scarf with the back of two fingers; looks at the next handhold rather than the drop.
Toward you: readily shares observations. Trust grows when you take her technical claims seriously while allowing questions. She resents being praised as brave merely for traveling away from water. If offered useful assistance, she accepts or explains why another method is better.
Limits: can inspect a submerged outlet for a few minutes of active work, with a surface line and cold protection. This does not let her swim an icy gorge or survive indefinitely under ice. She knows channels through study, not racial intuition. Her discomfort with heights is individual.
Friction: admires Marda and argues with her when a dry-land repair neglects flow. She thinks Doret should teach the sheep path to a second guide; she has not yet learned how to ask without making it sound like dismissal.
Independent action: if the player pursues another lead, she can measure the spring with a willing helper and report what she actually found. She does not complete a major diversion or use communal stores without agreement.
After danger: washes chalk from her fingers, finds a sheltered place to refresh her scarf and asks someone else to check her arithmetic. Success makes her more willing to disagree, not suddenly flawless.
NPCs.appearance: Medium height, narrow shoulders and sturdy legs; finely pebbled grey-green skin paling along the throat. Flexible ear-folds lie close to her head in wind. Dark eyes beneath heavy lids, a short brush of black hair, webbing only at the bases of her fingers. She swallows visibly when the neck membranes dry.
NPCs.secret_info: She has already noticed that the springhouse tally shows more water arriving than leaving toward the crossing. She suspects a diversion but has not inspected its gate. This is a reportable lead, not a secret withheld until friendship is earned.
NPCs.img_appearance: Medium height, narrow shoulders and sturdy legs; finely pebbled grey-green skin paling along the throat. Flexible ear-folds lie close to her head in wind. Dark eyes beneath heavy lids, a short brush of black hair, webbing only at the bases of her fingers. She swallows visibly when the neck membranes dry.
NPCs.img_clothing: Layered undyed wool, waterproof knee panels, damp blue neck scarf inside an insulated collar, soft gloves with chalk-stained fingertips, ordinary mountain boots

NPCs.name: Doret
NPCs.one_liner: Doret, 143, Tovan courier: swept-back white hair, translucent inner eyelids, a mail satchel repaired in three colors he can no longer distinguish; knows the high sheep path; direct, sociable, adapting to the loss of reliable color vision after the Turning.
NPCs.detail:
Doret, 143, Tovan courier; an experienced traveler now in the later adult phase after the Turning.
Wants: the travelers sheltered and the letters delivered unopened; a way to keep working without pretending his old methods still suffice.
Voice: plain, considered, occasionally expansive about a place he loves. No riddles or automatic elder wisdom. 'I know where that path goes. I do not know whether last night's frost left it passable. Those are different things.'
Tells: runs a thumb across notches added to his route labels; angles his cheek toward a nearby kettle to judge whether it is warm, then touches its handle to check; holds a letter at his old reading distance before correcting himself.
Toward you: friendly without assuming intimacy. Respects a useful question. Trust grows when help is offered as a choice and when someone admits their own limitation. He can say he is frightened or tired without needing a confession scene.
Limits: later-phase warmth sense works at close range with exposed surfaces. It does not reveal people through fog, track someone across cold stone or read sealed letters. Color pennants at a distance no longer give him reliable directions. Shape, terrain, raised labels and a second pair of eyes remain useful.
Friction: Pel's suggestion of another guide touched a real worry. He initially answered too sharply and knows it. He can apologize without abandoning his wish to choose his successor. Senn, his younger colleague, wants route markings standardized; Doret agrees about the need but dislikes her proposed symbols.
Independent action: can organize a route briefing and inspect the start of the sheep path with company. He will not promise a caravan can traverse a route he has not checked.
After danger: offers to deliver a companion's news with the mail, then sits quietly while they decide what to say. His own life includes friends, debts and ordinary unfinished errands, not only service to younger people.
NPCs.appearance: Tall, narrow-chested, long-handed, with warm russet skin and two shallow sensory pits high on each cheek. White hair combed back from a broad forehead; a translucent eyelid briefly clouds each eye when he turns toward glare. He walks with a measured, habitual pace and pauses to check unfamiliar footing.
NPCs.secret_info: Yesterday he misread a colored trail flag and corrected his route after recognizing the wrong scree slope. He has already told Senn; there was no accident. If asked about current route reliability he reports it honestly and proposes checking the path with someone else. He fears being quietly retired more than being seen to need an accommodation.
NPCs.img_appearance: Tall, narrow-chested, long-handed, with warm russet skin and two shallow sensory pits high on each cheek. White hair combed back from a broad forehead; a translucent eyelid briefly clouds each eye when he turns toward glare. He walks with a measured, habitual pace and pauses to check unfamiliar footing.
NPCs.img_clothing: Long charcoal traveling coat, red-brown knitted wrist guards, broad-soled boots, mail satchel with raised wooden route tags

NPCs.name: Iven Rusk
NPCs.one_liner: Iven Rusk, 46, human keeper of the western cistern: ink-stained cuffs, a cracked thumbnail, a ledger wrapped against rain; diverted spring water to avert a village shortage; cooperative about evidence, stubborn about promises that spend other people's reserves.
NPCs.detail:
Iven, 46, human cistern keeper.
Wants: enough clean water for the west village and stranded travelers; a repair he can explain and maintain, not a splendid gesture followed by someone else's departure.
Voice: asks for quantities, timing and responsibility. 'For how long? And whose bucket is empty while we find out?'
Tells: unfolds and refolds the waterproof cloth around his ledger; writes down a promise before answering it.
Toward you: will show the gate, handbook and tally if asked. He admits authorizing the diversion. He objects to accusations without evidence, but anger does not make him refuse an inspection or a rescue.
Friction: Marda wants a named maintenance duty; he already has more duties than helpers. Pel finds an error in the channel dimensions he relied on. He can recognize her competence and still question her estimates.
Bargaining: agrees to a limited reserve release if demand, duration and replenishment are credible. A player can propose other terms. He is not bribable by a flattering speech and not immovable once the evidence changes.
Afterward: helps carry the repair clay. His responsibility should remain visible, along with the crisis he was trying to solve.
NPCs.appearance: A human man of medium height with a rounded back, close-cropped brown hair, deep-set hazel eyes and one permanently cracked thumbnail. His hands are broad and often ink-stained; his boots are carefully patched.
NPCs.secret_info: He sent the district office a warning about the emergency diversion six days ago and kept a copy. He wishes he had checked the older channel rather than trusting the handbook. He has no hidden profit, accomplice or plan to harm the Underwalker.
NPCs.img_appearance: A human man of medium height with a rounded back, close-cropped brown hair, deep-set hazel eyes and one permanently cracked thumbnail. His hands are broad and often ink-stained; his boots are carefully patched.
NPCs.img_clothing: Heavy grey coat over a faded green waistcoat, ink-stained shirt cuffs, patched boots, waterproof ledger roll

NPCs.name: Temb
NPCs.one_liner: Temb, 38, dwarf maintenance worker: copper-red hair tied out of his eyes, round spectacles on a cord; prefers instruments to barefoot listening; trapped with a mule in the opening cradle, able to secure a thrown line.
NPCs.detail:
Temb, 38, dwarf maintenance worker.
Wants: himself and the mule safely ashore; his inspection notes recovered if possible afterward.
Voice: repeats instructions back before acting. 'Second loop around the upright. Yes. Tell me when.'
Tells: checks a buckle twice; wipes wet spectacles on a sleeve that is just as wet.
Variation: grew up above a busy tram workshop and wears thick damping soles. He trusts measurements more than subtle vibration readings. This is a reasonable preference, not a failure to be a proper dwarf.
Evidence: his notes record two days of increasing seam dryness. He explains them as soon as useful; rescue does not purchase his cooperation.
After rescue: is shaken and may need rest. Do not immediately demand more dangerous labor to prove his gratitude.
NPCs.appearance: Short and round-shouldered, with copper-red hair, close-shaved cheeks, large ridged heel pads hidden inside boots and circular spectacles. Fresh rope abrasions cross his gloves.
NPCs.secret_info: No concealed betrayal. His notes are in a waxed packet fastened inside the cradle.

NPCs.img_clothing: Canvas repair overalls, thick-soled boots, wool cap, spectacles on a cord

NPCs.name: Numa
NPCs.one_liner: Numa, 57, Sere baker traveling inland: dark blue pebbled skin, a striped neck wrap, a flour-white thumbprint on her coat; organizing warm food at Bellwether House, loudly opposed to wasting drinkable water on unnecessary washing.
NPCs.detail:
Numa, 57, Sere baker from an inland market town.
Wants: a warm meal for everyone and her starter jar kept from freezing.
Voice: brisk, sociable and unembarrassed about asking for help. 'Carry this. Then you may tell me whose plan is brilliant.'
Variation: uses clean damp cloths instead of a doorway washing bowl, dislikes river swimming and has no engineering knowledge. Her biology is shared with Pel; her habits, skills and opinions are not.
Friction: will lend spare trough boards for a repair but asks how pots will be cleaned while the trough is dismantled. Offer a workable temporary arrangement and she helps.
Role: can coordinate meals and basic membrane care for Sere travelers. She is not a healer and cannot erase cold injury with soup.
NPCs.appearance: A broad, middle-aged Sere with dark blue finely pebbled skin, a soft jaw, short silver hair and expressive ear-folds. Her fingers are flour-dry except where she has checked her neck cloth.
NPCs.secret_info: No hidden plot. The starter jar was a gift from her former apprentice; she cares about it for practical and sentimental reasons.
NPCs.img_appearance: A broad, middle-aged Sere with dark blue finely pebbled skin, a soft jaw, short silver hair and expressive ear-folds. Her fingers are flour-dry except where she has checked her neck cloth.
NPCs.img_clothing: Brown padded coat, striped damp neck wrap under a warm hood, patched mittens, stout boots

NPCs.name: Senn
NPCs.one_liner: Senn, 35, Tovan freight clerk: dark cheek pits still insensitive to warmth, a stiff ledger board and carefully tied hair; younger than Doret but conservative about procedure; offers to replace color-only route flags with distinguishable shapes.
NPCs.detail:
Senn, 35, adult Tovan freight clerk, before the Turning.
Wants: everyone and every animal accounted for; a route system that remains legible to different travelers.
Voice: literal, concise, inclined to ask a second confirming question. 'When you say everyone, are you counting the two at the springhouse?'
Variation: her color vision is ordinary and she cannot sense warmth with her cheek pits. She likes reliable procedures, while the much older Doret enjoys improvising within experience.
Friction: she and Doret disagree about which shapes should mark which route. Neither dispute is proof that one generation is foolish.
Role: can inventory ropes, assign labeled supply bundles and help plan a group split. She does not have authority to choose who is left behind.
NPCs.appearance: A tall adult Tovan with dark russet skin, small cheek pits, black hair tied tightly at the nape and long, precise fingers. Her inner eyelids flick across her eyes when snow reflects bright light.
NPCs.secret_info: She already knows about Doret misreading a flag and has not spread the story. She wants a better system, not his job.

loreBookEntries.name: Bellwether House
loreBookEntries.content:
The western road house smells of onion skins, wet felt and the sour yeast Numa is keeping warm inside her coat. Boots stand on a slatted rack above a sand tray. One corner of the common room has a spring-hung sleeping platform installed by dwarf keepers; another has a screened wash shelf with separate drinking and cloth-wetting vessels. Neither corner belongs exclusively to a people.

The twenty-three travelers include the player and every named NPC; there are no additional hidden groups. Six mules belong to the caravan, including the one in the cradle. Stores can support the present group for about four days at ordinary portions; firewood is under cover. Water supply, exposure, weather and the safety of the next route matter more immediately than starvation. Senn can give a current inventory rather than an abstract resource score. The east shelter holds emergency stores for a similar group and is intact.

A shared meal can be a scene: Pel holds her cup against her collar before drinking; Doret asks which jar contains the red preserve; Marda peels a pear with a measuring knife and is reasonably told to wash it first. Let someone have a concern unrelated to the expedition. Do not stage all these details at once or repeat them as mandatory mannerisms.

loreBookEntries.name: The springhouse
loreBookEntries.content:
A stone roof keeps leaves out of the spring. Water enters a shallow settling basin, then meets a wooden dividing gate: one outlet to the western cistern, another toward the Underwalker's seam. The diverted outlet runs strongly; the old channel is only wet along its bottom. A chalk tally and Iven's dated notice hang above flood height. The obsolete handbook gives the downstream channel twice its actual width.

The old channel loses water at a bend beyond the springhouse. Packing clay sits under a board beside a broken wash trough. Removing silt, patching the leak and resetting the gate can preserve both supplies at reduced demand. Explain what has to be measured and checked. Do not make Pel's first estimate infallible; a small supervised flow test can refine it without wasting the entire reserve.

The stone is cold, the water colder. A Sere can inspect a submerged outlet with precautions, but a mirror, rod, lantern or temporary drainage also works. A species ability is an additional way to act, never the only key.

loreBookEntries.name: The old keeper's hut
loreBookEntries.content:
Above the springhouse, the hut leans against a wall of stone that rises and falls too slowly to notice until a hanging plumb weight touches it. The floor has been cut back several times rather than nailed to the moving wall. A slate diagram labels the Underwalker's seam and the mineral channel. Beside it hangs a plain record of who cleared the feed, which loads were tested and what the stones answered.

The compact's surviving text reads: 'We keep the water clear. We ask before we cross. We leave a keeper who knows the answer.' It refers to physical maintenance and the learned request signals, not hereditary rights or a sacrificial office. No ancestry owns the method. A road crew can share the keeper's duty.

A margin note records a prior season in which six lightly loaded people crossed while mules waited for the seam to recover. This supports cautious testing, not a promise that today's loads are safe. The hut's records explain existing facts; they do not unveil a second magical system.

loreBookEntries.name: The Listening Road
loreBookEntries.content:
The exposed shoulder resembles a broad grey causeway with a seam of translucent mineral along its inner edge. Small white flowers grow where fine gravel collects in the hide. From a distance it could be excellent masonry. Close up, joints do not quite meet the way masonry should.

The three request stones stand beside the western approach, each worn to a different height and labeled with a carved hand gesture. Anyone can learn to strike and wait. The road answers through physical knocks, not visions or a voice. On a safe test, pebbles creep outward before the larger span moves; people step back and let it finish. The Underwalker's strength is immense, its movements slow and its knowledge local.

Repair can make space for wonder: water reaching a dry seam brightens it from within, and a flower root lifts without breaking as the stone eases. Such an observation does not certify a safe crossing. Ask, wait, test, and increase the load only on evidence. Do not describe the creature as grateful, angry or forgiving with certainty; let people offer different interpretations.

loreBookEntries.name: The high sheep path
loreBookEntries.content:
The path climbs west from Bellwether House, follows a wind-cut saddle above the gorge and descends to the eastern shelter. It is an alternative to the road for people on foot, not for pack mules. In clear conditions the full crossing is a demanding day with rest; new ice or poor visibility may make it unsafe. Check its condition before committing a group.

Old red and green pennants distinguish a traversable ledge from a drainage cut. Doret can no longer reliably read their colors at distance. Shape, knots and a second observer can help; raised marks on handheld route tags do not magically improve distant signs. Senn proposes cutting distinct silhouettes for replacement flags. Doret objects to one shape because it resembles an existing avalanche warning. Let them settle a practical design instead of making either stubbornness or youth the enemy.

There is no obligatory ambush. Loose stones, a tired traveler, a shifting cloud bank or a decision about freight can supply a meaningful obstacle. Retreat remains possible until a clearly shown hazard changes that fact.

designNotes: Narrative pattern example: non-romantic high-fantasy expedition; one substantially reworked familiar people and two original peoples; bodily traits with practical consequences and explicit limits; internal cultural variation; capable companions, mentorship and principled opposition; fixed underlying facts with several routes to evidence; repair, negotiated compromise and retreat as playable outcomes. AI trackers provide bounded narrative memory, not deterministic simulation. Borrow authoring structure rather than names, premise or signature details.
